# Evaluating the Ability to Consent to Research: a Twenty-Year Track Record

## Abstract

Occasionally, the ability of prospective research participants to consent may be uncertain. The simple use of standardized capacity assessment tools may not suffice to determine the ability to consent to a particular research protocol. This study consisted of a retrospective review of the outcomes of an alternative approach used by the Ability-to-Consent Assessment Team at the National Institutes of Health. Of 944 individuals evaluated over 20 years (1999–2019), 70.1% were determined to have capacity. Of those who lacked capacity to consent and were subsequently evaluated for their ability to assign a surrogate, 86.0% had the ability to do so. The findings demonstrate that establishing a task-specific approach for assessing the capacity of potential participants to consent to a variety of research protocols can facilitate safe and ethically justifiable inclusion of research participants whose ability to consent is initially uncertain.

## Introduction

Research regarding conditions that can cause cognitive impairment is of vital importance. Such studies provide the opportunity to improve methods to prevent, treat and possibly cure conditions that cause significant morbidity to millions of people. To understand the nature of diagnoses associated with cognitive impairment, investigators may need to conduct research with individuals who are not able to provide informed consent. In addition to instances where it is anticipated that some individuals may be cognitively impaired (e.g. Alzheimer’s disease), potential research participants are occasionally candidates for enrollment in protocols to study conditions that are not cognitively impairing but have cognitive impairment due to other comorbidities. Proceeding with the ethical enrollment of individuals under both sets of circumstances requires a careful evaluation of their capacity to consent and possible use of surrogate consent. The Common Rule1 recommends safeguards for the enrollment of individuals who cannot consent in non-emergency research through surrogate consent and in doing so serves to protect these individuals.

A key concern when considering research enrollment under these circumstances is that researchers may occasionally be in doubt about the ability of prospective research participants to consent. Consent capacity may be uncertain due to developmental delay (including individuals who may have never had consent capacity); or may be diminished due to a gradually deteriorating degenerative condition; and/or may fluctuate due to a psychiatric or neurologic condition; or it may be temporarily diminished due to some other unstable medical condition. Validated assessment tools using explicit criteria that track specific cognitive abilities constitutive of capacity exist. Such tools are most commonly used for the assessment of individuals with dementia or psychiatric conditions. A 2017 review of assessment tools evaluating older patients’ capacity to consent showed 14 tools that were considered appropriate for use in the setting of clinical research2. The MacArthur Competence Assessment Tool for Clinical Research (MacCAT-CR) was the best validated and most frequently used3. However, the widespread use of such tools has been criticized because they may not be well-designed for assessment of the capacity to make particular decisions4. For example, the use of a numerical score to define incapacity may not be appropriate for judging an individual’s ability to make decisions in circumstances that vary in terms of complexity and risk.

Many medical institutions that conduct a large number of clinical trials can expect to have potential participants who may lack decisional capacity. Yet few institutions have staff who are trained and prepared to evaluate the decisional capacity of potential research participants when the need arises. The Secretary’s Advisory Committee on Human Research Protections (SACHRP) Subcommittee on Inclusion of Individuals with Impaired Decision-making in Research estimated in 2009 that 5 million Americans were diagnosed with Alzheimer’s disease, nearly 800,000 strokes occurred in the U.S. each year, and 50,000 patients were admitted to intensive care units each day and that these three conditions associated with impaired consent capacity were destined to become more prevalent as the population ages (SACHRP Subcommittee on the Inclusion of Individuals with Impaired Decision-Making in Research SIIIDR 2009). Without the means to evaluate the capacity to consent and to find alternative avenues for surrogate consent, institutions are likely to forgo enrollment of persons who lack capacity.

To address the need for a systematic approach to assess potential research participants whose ability to consent may be uncertain, the National Institutes of Health Clinical Center (NIH CC) has a consultation service, the Ability to Consent Assessment Team (ACAT) that evaluates whether persons have the capacity to consent and, if not, whether they still retain sufficient cognitive abilities to be able to assign a surrogate decision-maker. The ACAT also evaluates whether assigned surrogates are appropriate persons to make decisions on behalf of an incapacitated prospective participant. Having such a consultation service that is independent of research personnel can be useful because it is likely to be freer of conflicts of interests than the research team, and may therefore be able to provide a more objective assessment by virtue of their distance from the research5. Furthermore, such consultants have special training and experience in performing capacity assessments that research teams are unlikely to have. Such a consultation service can play a crucial role in the conduct of ethically responsible clinical research and serve an important protective function by keeping incapacitated adults from being inappropriately enrolled in or excluded from research.

The primary purpose of this study is to examine the outcomes of capacity assessments administered to a large sample of individuals by an experienced team using a routinized process to assess the ability to provide informed consent for research. The study addressed several questions regarding factors that might influence judgments about the ability to consent to research: How frequently was research enrollment that would otherwise not have been ethically permissible because of possible lack of ability to consent, facilitated by routine use of a capacity assessment team? How many individuals who lacked the capacity to consent were nonetheless able to assign a surrogate for consent on their behalf? Are potential research participants, whose capacity is assessed for reasons related to their individual circumstances, more likely to lack capacity than potential research participants who are required to have a capacity assessment as a routine part of a protocol? Are potential research participants who are enrolling in lower risk or potentially beneficial research more likely to be assessed as able to consent?

## Methods

### Setting

The NIH CC is the largest hospital dedicated solely to research in North America. It has approximately 1500 ongoing research protocols6. In 2019, there were approximately 100,000 outpatient visits and 5,000 inpatient admissions7.

### Study design

This study involved a retrospective chart review spanning over 20 years (7/29/99 to 12/31/19) of the internal service records of the Bioethics Consultation Service (BCS) run by the Department of Bioethics, and the Human Subjects Protection Unit (HSPU) under the auspices of the NIMH Office of the Clinical Director. These two services evaluate potential research participants either independently or together. At times, individuals from these two services function together as the ACAT, providing services throughout the CC to both inpatients and outpatients. Staff of the BCS are experienced in research ethics consultation. Staff of the HSPU are experienced as advocates for research participants. The ACAT is thus comprised of individuals with advanced degrees and training related to enrolling populations in research who may not be able to consent for themselves. Capacity assessment requests are sometimes called to assess for and manage a medical etiology (e.g. delirium); these requests are referred to the Psychiatry Consultation Liaison Service and were not included in the database analyzed here.

Each of these services retained records of capacity assessments for potential participants who had questionable capacity to consent or who were considering enrollment in a research protocol that required capacity assessment for all enrollees. These records include details of how the evaluations were performed, assessment criteria for capacity, information about the participants and protocols, and the outcome of each evaluation. These records were originally created to facilitate a record of services provided rather than for research purposes.

### Study population

While the NIH CC enrolls both children and adults, our study focuses on adults. The study population included: 1) all potential adult research participants referred to the ACAT whose capacity to consent was considered uncertain by a member of the research team or based on IRB requirement because of a condition that might be associated with the loss of ability to consent, and 2) surrogate decision-makers assessed for appropriateness to provide consent.

### NIH CC policy and practices of the ACAT

The NIH CC Medical Administrative Series (MAS) policy 87–4 was implemented March 30, 1987 and outlined the consent process for clinical research for participants who are or will become cognitively impaired. In 2018, MAS 87–4 was replaced by Office of Human Subjects Research Protections (OHSRP) with Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) 14E: Research Involving Adults Who Lack Decision-Making Capacity to Consent to Research Participation. Subsequent to the completion of data extraction for this study, in 2020, Policy 4038 was implemented in the course of reorganization and consolidation of intramural NIH IRBs. These policies are compatible with the Code of Federal Regulations Title 45 part 46 and guide appropriate additional safeguards to a variety of protocols and research populations throughout the NIH CC.

While NIH CC policy was updated over time, core elements remain constant. The policy sets forth investigator and IRB responsibilities when considering the enrollment of participants without decision-making capacity and when consultation is required. The policy specifies that each research protocol will describe and the IRB may approve the following: justification for inclusion of participant unable to provide consent, how the ability to provide consent will be assessed, how the permission of an appropriate surrogate will be obtained, the risk of the research and likelihood of benefit (if any) for adults unable to consent, procedures for obtaining assent and respecting dissent as well as any additional safeguards.

Use of surrogate consent is based on categories of risk and benefit. For example, legal guardians, agents of durable power of attorneys (DPAs) for healthcare and next of kin (NOK) are approvable by the IRB for minimal risk or prospect of direct benefit protocols. In 2008, the NIH policy added an additional category of risk - minor increment over minimal risk without a prospect of direct benefit category which allows legal guardians and agents of DPA but not NOK to enroll participants. More than a minor increase over minimal risk protocols without a prospect of direct benefit do not allow surrogate consent unless additional outside review requirements have been met.

NIH CC policy states that in the case of a legal guardian providing consent, the guardianship decree must be reviewed by legal counsel to ensure the state which issued the guardianship allows for the proposed research as categories of allowable research varies depending on jurisdiction.

Some adults who are unable to consent for themselves and do not have a previously assigned surrogate or legal guardian may still be capable of assigning a surrogate through an NIH advance directive (AD). In this case, NIH CC policy also stipulates that the ACAT (vs investigator) must make this assessment. Similarly, in the case of NOK consent, the appropriateness of the surrogate assessments are performed by ACAT.

### The ACAT assessments

IRBs range in their interpretations of appropriate assessment and protections for enrolling research participants who may not have consent capacity. The published literature reports an array of documentation practices, tools used, domains assessed and levels of training of the person making the assessment9. Reviews of instruments used to assess capacity most often cite the MacCAT-CR10. The University of California, San Diego Brief Assessment of Capacity to Consent (UBACC)11 is a brief screening tool which identifies when a more in-depth capacity assessment is indicated. The ACAT tools lay somewhere in the middle of these two assessments: ACAT creates and administers tools based on the MacCAT-CR3 but more closely resembles the UCBACC in terms of length and time taken to administer.

The ACAT utilizes two types of capacity assessments: protocol-specific assessments and generic assessments that are not protocol specific. A protocol-specific capacity assessment is used when a protocol routinely requires some or all potential participants to be formally assessed prior to consenting because the research team and IRB anticipate a high probability of incapacity to consent among the study population. It is created in advance of participants enrolling and expected responses to questions have been developed. The generic capacity assessment is used as a guide for an assessment of individuals who are being considered for enrollment in a protocol that normally does not enroll cognitively impaired individuals. It consists of generic questions, and respondent answers are expected to be appropriate to the protocol in question. Examples similar to these tools can be found in the NIMH Human Subjects Research Protections Toolkit, Section 212.

These tools were not validated by comparison with any gold-standard. Rather, they have face validity in that they include questions pertaining to the domains of capacity to consent: understanding, appreciation, reasoning, and choice. Both protocol-specific and generic assessment tools assess the four domains through a series of 9 to 11 open-ended questions which may lead to further follow-up questions. Tailored questions pertain to the aforementioned domains: understanding of the potential participant’s personal situation (e.g., What is the illness/medical concern that has brought you here?), study specific procedures (e.g., What will you be asked to do as part of this study?), risks and benefits (e.g., What are the most important risks to you? How do you feel about participating in research that is designed to help others in the future), and, alternatives (e.g., What are the differences between being in this research and other treatment options?); appreciation of the effects of study participation on the potential participant’s personal situation (e.g., Will you have to stop any current treatments or medications?); reasoning of why the potential participant wants to be in research (e.g., Why do you think participating in this study is the better option for you?); and choice (e.g., Whose decision is it to enroll in this study and what would happen if you didn’t?).

Capacity assessments are conducted only after the potential participant has been educated about the protocol i.e. they have talked to the investigator and had the opportunity to read the consent forms. The number of people in the room are kept to a minimum. Additional observers such as staff, or family members are carefully considered and justified in order to keep potential stress and anxiety on the part of the potential participant at a minimum as well as to prevent outside influences on potential participant answers (e.g., cuing or perceived pressure to answer in a certain way).

The thresholds on sufficiency for each of the aforementioned domains are, with rare exception, based on the judgements by two evaluators who must reach an agreement. Each evaluator rates the potential participant’s answers to questions pertaining to the four domains (e.g., understand, has partial understanding, does not understand) and then makes an overall assessment of the individual’s capacity to provide informed consent. The two evaluators then discuss and resolve any differences in their assessments and make a final determination. If the evaluators find the potential is able to give informed consent, the researcher may proceed with obtaining informed consent. If the potential subject is found to have questionable ability (e.g., difficulty in 1–2 domains); or the potential subject is determined unable to give informed consent (e.g., difficulty in multiple domains or severe difficulty in 1 domain); or there is disagreement between evaluators, then proceeding with the consent process was not advised. The researcher then may decide to: educate the potential participant further and re-assess for consent capacity; to pursue surrogate consent (if allowed by protocol); or not enroll the individual into that protocol. The outcomes are conveyed to the potential participant, family member (if applicable), research team and documented in the medical record.

The ACAT Ability to Assign a Surrogate Decision-Maker Assessment consists of questions designed to ascertain whether the potential participant understands: that the goal of research is to learn something that may help others, some or all of the research procedures may offer no chance of individual benefit, research procedures can involve discomfort and risk, decisions about research participation and the procedures done as part of the research will be made by the surrogate, and that the participant retains the right to say “no” research. The participant must be able to identify a person to make decisions for them while in a protocol13.

The Surrogate Decision-Maker Assessment evaluates whether the assigned surrogate sufficiently understands that the protocol involves research; the risks, benefits, and alternatives, that participation is consistent with the participant’s values, preferences and interests; and is comfortable, willing and able to serve as substitute decision-maker14. As is the case when assessing the capacity of a potential research participant to consent to research, the Ability to Assign a Surrogate Decision-Maker and Surrogate Assessments involve two evaluators unless otherwise indicated.

### Data extraction methods

Data were extracted from the records of HSPU and BCS and subsequently added to an Excel document database. The data collected for this study included: ID recorded in service records, date of consult, which consult service performed the assessment (HSPU, BCS or ACAT), what assessment tool was used (either protocol specific or generic), language spoken during the evaluation (English was assumed unless use of an interpreter was mentioned), whether it was a single or repeat assessment on the same protocol, demographics of the participants (initials, age, gender identification, diagnosis, diagnostic category), study information (protocol, institute, whether the IRB required the capacity assessment, whether the protocol permitted surrogate consent), assessment outcomes (whether or not the potential participant was deemed to have the ability to consent for admission to the NIH CC, to research, to treatment, to designate a surrogate and whether the surrogate was evaluated and found to be appropriate) and surrogate information (whether potential participant had a legal guardian, a DPA for healthcare or a NOK). In addition, data were collected regarding the specific protocol(s) for which each participant was evaluated. These data were collected from the consultation records or in cases where this information was missing, it was collected from the IRB of record for the relevant protocol.

### Research protection

This study was approved by the NHGRI IRB. This retrospective record review did not involve contact with research participants. No personally identifying information was collected. Consent was therefore not obtained.

### Data analysis

Descriptive statistics were used to analyze the characteristics of the study population, research protocols, and outcomes of capacity assessments.

Data were analyzed to examine several hypotheses: 1) some individuals who lack the capacity to consent are nonetheless able to assign a surrogate who can consent on their behalf; 2) potential research participants who are assessed during pro re nata (PRN) capacity assessments are more likely to lack capacity than potential research participants who are required to have a capacity assessment as a routine part of a protocol; 3) the level of risk and benefit of a study may be correlated with the likelihood that the individuals will be evaluated as able to consent; and 4) some research enrollment that would otherwise not have been ethically permissible because of possible lack of ability to consent may be permissible through IRB approved surrogate consent and facilitated by routine use of a capacity assessment team.

Finally, the study examined factors associated with the capacity to consent to research and the capacity to assign a surrogate in bivariate (one explanatory variable at a time) and multivariable analyses (“best” set of explanatory variables). Because of the presence of repeated measures, and the response variables being nominal in the case of capacity to consent (yes, no or questionable), and binary in the case of capacity to assign a surrogate (yes or no), these analyses were based on generalized estimating equations (GEE).15 In the bivariate analyses, the model-fit quasi-likelihood information criteria (QIC)16 were compared with and without the explanatory variable to determine whether each explanatory variable was associated with each of the two response variables. The “best” set of patient characteristics, the “best” set of protocol and assessment characteristics, and the “best” combination of patient and protocol characteristics that are associated with each of the two response variables were determined based on the model with the lowest QIC. In all analyses, age represents the age of the participant at the time of the consult service. It was included separately in statistical models as a continuous variable, and or a categorical variable with six age groups: 18–29, 30–39, 40–49, 50–59, 60–69 and ≥70.

## Results

### Study population

There were 944 prospective research participants who were evaluated in capacity assessments during the study time period (7/29/99 to 12/31/19), (Table 1). Most were in the youngest age range (18 – 29 years) while the remainder were evenly distributed among other age ranges. More men (61.4%) were evaluated than women (37.2%) with 1.4% unspecified. The most common diagnostic categories for the diseases mentioned in the assessment notes or in the eligibility criteria of the protocols in which the potential participants were enrolling were, in order of prevalence, neurologic diseases (36.1%), mental illness (26.3%), substance use disorders (6.1%), neoplastic diseases (6.0%), infectious diseases (4.7%), and developmentally delaying conditions (4.0%). The distribution of diagnoses across the age groups can be seen in Figure 1.

### Features of capacity assessments

A total of 1436 assessments were reviewed. Of these, 1178 assessments were performed with potential research participants: 1135 were assessments of capacity to consent to research, 34 were assessments of capacity to consent to clinical care, 10 were assessments of ability to consent to admission to the Clinical Center, and 257 were assessments of ability to assign a surrogate (Table 3). Of the 1436 total assessments, 258 were performed with potential surrogates to assess their appropriateness as surrogate decision-makers. The majority (60.7%) of the assessments of potential research participants were administered for NIMH protocols, and 96.7% of assessments of potential research participants were conducted in English (Table 2).

### Ability to consent

In 1135 assessments of the capacity to consent to research, 840 (74.0%) individuals were determined to be able to consent (Table 3). In bivariate analyses pertaining to individual characteristics, age (continuous) was not associated with capacity to consent, while gender, age group, diagnostic category and language spoken were. Regarding gender, 71.9% of females and 75.0% of males were found to be able to consent (Table 4). Regarding association between age and ability to consent, individuals in the 40–49 year age bracket were the most likely to be able to consent (84.7%) and those in the age brackets 18–29 and ≥70 were least likely to be able to consent (69.2% and 68.5%, respectively). Potential participants whose spoken language was not English and required an interpreter were less likely to have the ability to consent (31.4%) compared to potential participants who spoke English (75.4%). Assessments of individuals whose conditions were in developmental disease diagnostic categories were the least likely to find that individuals were able to consent (13.5%) and assessments of those individuals with mental illnesses and substance use disorders were the most likely to find that individuals were able to consent (88.3% and 98.4% respectively), (Table 4).

In bivariate analyses regarding protocol characteristics, all four characteristics were associated with the capacity to consent. The NIH Institutes associated with greater capacity to consent to research were NCI, NHLBI, NIAAA, NIMH and NINDS. Assessments required by the IRB were also associated with a greater capacity to consent to research than those assessments that were done on an as needed basis (83.3% vs. 53.8%), (Table 5).

In multivariable analysis including the 4 potential participant characteristics, the set of characteristics most highly associated with capacity to consent to research only included the diagnostic category. From among the 4 protocol characteristics, the “best” set of characteristics associated with capacity to consent to research included the NIH institute and whether the IRB required a capacity assessment. From among the combined eight potential participant and protocol characteristics, the “best” set of predictors of capacity to consent to research included the diagnostic category and the IRB-designated benefit level of the protocol.

### Ability to assign a surrogate

In bivariate analysis of participant characteristics, the ability to assign a surrogate was associated with the age (continuous) of the potential participants. The younger the age, the less able to assign a surrogate. In bivariate analysis of the protocol characteristics, the protocol risk level and IRB requirement of a capacity assessment were associated with ability to assign a surrogate: 92.2% of potential participants assessed for more than minimal risk protocols had the ability to assign a surrogate compared to 79.1% for minimal risk protocols, and 93.4% of potential participants assessed for protocols for which the IRB required an assessment for the capacity to consent had the ability to assign a surrogate compared to 84.2% when the IRB did not require the capacity assessment. In multivariate analysis, from among the 8 potential participant and protocol characteristics, the best predictor of the ability to assign a surrogate remained the protocol’s risk level.

### Outcomes of study hypotheses

This study set out to explore and address four study hypotheses as outlined in the Data analysis subsection in Methods. In testing hypothesis 1 regarding the association between level or risk and benefit of a study with the likelihood that individuals will be evaluated as able to consent, in bivariate analysis that assessments for protocols with no direct benefit were associated with greater capacity to consent to research (80.1%) than protocols with some prospect of direct benefit (53.8%), and that assessments for protocols that were assigned more than minimal risk levels were associated with greater likelihood of capacity (79.7%) than assessments for protocols for minimal or unspecified risk levels (49.3%). Multivariable analysis showed a persistent association between benefit level and ability to consent to research whereas risk level was no longer associated with ability to consent to research.

In testing hypothesis 2 regarding PRN capacity assessments, 83.3% of potential participants who were considered for enrollment in protocols that required capacity assessments (N=777) had the ability to consent to research while only 53.8% of potential participants considered for enrollment in protocols that didn’t require capacity assessments as a routine part of the protocol (N=346) had the ability to consent to research.

In testing hypothesis 3 that some individuals who lack the capacity to consent are nonetheless able to assign a surrogate who can consent on their behalf, the data showed that 86.0% of 257 assessments, individuals were determined to have this ability (Table 3).

In testing hypothesis 4, among the study sample of individuals who were brought to the attention of a capacity assessment team at the NIH because of doubts about their ability to consent to research, 1,053 of 1135 assessments were found to be eligible for enrollment in research either through consent on their own (N=796) or consent by a surrogate of their choice (N=257).

## Discussion

This study was conducted to characterize the process and outcomes of the ACAT at the NIH CC, a team that has been routinely used for 20 years when the ability of potential research participants to consent has been in doubt. The majority (74.3%) of the individuals who were assessed were judged able to consent. Many (86.0%) of the potential research participants who were judged unable to consent were nonetheless considered able to assign a surrogate to consent on their behalf. The consequence is that research including a substantial percentage of individuals whose research enrollment would have been ethically impermissible otherwise was facilitated by routine use of an experienced capacity assessment team that is free of conflicts of interest that research teams might have. The alternate pathways to enrollment that were recommended included surrogate consent by previously assigned DPA, DPA assigned at the time of the capacity assessment, or NOK.

The study findings suggest that when a clinical investigator, research nurse or social worker has doubts about a potential research participant’s cognitive ability, it is not possible to predict on the basis of the participant’s personal characteristics - including a combination of their gender, age and illness – whether they are likely to be able to consent. While some diagnostic categories associated with developmental impairment are associated with less likely ability to consent, this is far from a certain predictor. The findings show that assessment of the elements of capacity to consent – understanding, appreciation, reasoning, and ability to communicate a choice – tailored to the proposed research protocol can serve as a reasonable determination of whether an individual has capacity to consent as well as capacity to designate a surrogate who can consent on their behalf.

In the course of doing this review a number of protocols were found for which IRBs or investigators did not specify whether surrogates could act to give surrogate consent which meant that the number of surrogate assessments that were conducted was lower than might have been otherwise allowed and thus a number of potential participants were thus not given the opportunity to enroll. Therefore even with a consultation service in place, the enrollment of participants is heavily reliant on the active attention and participation of the investigators in the process.

### Study limitations

This study was conducted at a single institution. Yet it did involve capacity assessments for individuals who were expected to enroll in over 215 protocols from 15 NIH institutes, most of which had separate IRBs. The study was a retrospective record review that posed several limitations. No personally identifiable information was available so some factors that might have been useful to explore could not be analyzed including years of education, race, and severity of symptoms associated with their diagnosis17. The internal service records were not linked with medical records so that while the ACAT judgement of each individual’s ability to consent could be gleaned, it was not possible to determine the subsequent course of action regarding research participation.

In addition, the convenience sample included in this study is a reflection of the diseases studied in protocols at the NIH intramural program and not a reflection of clinical research as a whole. For example, there were no protocols studying cerebrovascular accidents at the NIH CC, thus this common cause of cognitive impairment is absent from this study. Therefore the conclusions that can be drawn from this study are not entirely generalizable and the prevalence of the loss of capacity to consent to research in some diseases relative to others is not likely to be reproducible.

### Strengths

The study adds to the literature on research consent through its inclusion of individuals with a variety of medical conditions as well as its inclusion of a larger sample size than previous studies. Prior studies have largely focused on decisional capacity among potential research participants with neurologic and mental disorders and individuals who are 60 years of age or older18. Previous studies that aimed to assess the capacity to consent to research have also been largely limited to study designs involving hypothetical research enrollment19. In contrast, the results in this study involve individuals who were actually being considered for enrollment in clinical protocols. While hypothetical studies have the advantage of being able to hold variables constant, the findings here offer the advantage of revealing the complexities and nuances of actual research enrollment.

### Interpretation and implications of study findings

It is difficult to compare this study’s results with previous studies because of the variety of tools used for capacity-to-consent assessments, and the heterogeneity of scientific objectives and inclusion criteria entailed in the research protocols for which prospective research participants were being evaluated. Previous studies, in addition to mostly consisting of hypothetical scenarios, sometimes included participants who were young enough to exclude aging as a confounding variable20 while others only included participants who were 60 years or older21. In a previous study that compared the performance of individuals with various diagnoses, potential participants with Alzheimer’s Disease showed the worst performance on decision-making capacity followed by potential participants with schizophrenia and then by potential participants with diabetes mellitus22. Another study found that potential participants with schizophrenia performed worse than potential participants with HIV23. Our findings differ from the outcomes of these studies in that the percentage of potential participants who were able to consent were higher for neurologic disease than any other category. The results found here reflect the large proportion of assessments for neurologic disorders and mental illness that were IRB-mandated, meaning every potential participant was evaluated because of the IRB’s anticipation of the possibility of cognitive impairment for the study population as a whole, rather than because of a particular individual’s questionable ability to consent to research.

It can be inferred from this study finding, perhaps not surprisingly, that an IRB mandate to routinely perform capacity assessments as a safeguard to avoid enrollment of individuals who are cognitively impaired will lead to performance of far more assessments with a far lower rate of cognitive impairment.

While it was hypothesized that assessment team members might have a higher threshold for judging prospective research participants as having the capacity to consent to enrollment in research when the protocols offered no prospect of direct benefit to enrollees, the opposite was found to be the case. This finding may be due to investigators themselves screening out individuals who are unable to consent to non-beneficial research so that the ACAT team saw few of such individuals.

One concerning study finding was that individuals who did not speak English and required an interpreter during their assessment, were far less likely to be assessed as able to consent. It is not possible to determine whether this is due failure to overcome a language barrier, lack of education about and familiarity with medical research, inadequate preparatory explanations about the research protocol in which these individuals were going to enroll. Further exploration of these possibilities is needed.

When examining the association of factors with the ability to assign a surrogate, younger age and protocols with lower level of risk were associated with a lower ability to assign a surrogate. This finding is likely due to the fact that assessments of the ability to assign a surrogate were not performed for higher risk protocols that did not allow enrollment by surrogates. Thus the protocols included in the analysis of the Ability to Assign a Surrogate Decision-Maker Assessment outcomes are protocols with overall lower levels of risk. In particular, many young potential participants evaluated for enrollment in protocols studying schizophrenia were not evaluated for their ability to assign a surrogate. These potential participants fell under the mental illness diagnostic category (green bars in Figure 1). The schizophrenia protocols were judged as more than minimal risk by the IRB and surrogate consent was not permitted. Hence only two Ability to Assign a Surrogate Decision-Maker Assessments were conducted on this specific population.

Younger participants were also more likely to be evaluated for the ability to assign a surrogate because older age groups may have already completed an advance directive that assigned a surrogate decision-maker. This meant that for higher risk protocols, when potential participants lacked capacity to consent to research and were evaluated for their ability to assign a surrogate, younger participants were overrepresented. Therefore, one potential explanation for the association between ability to assign a surrogate and the risk level is the exclusion of participants who were enrolling in protocols that didn’t allow for enrollment through a NOK surrogates. The exclusion may have led to a skew in the assessments towards potential participants who were unlikely to lack the ability to assign a surrogate.

Additionally, a total of 41 assessments for the Ability to Assign a Surrogate Decision-Maker were completed even when surrogate consent was not allowed by the protocol. They were completed either as a safeguard for potential loss of capacity or because the potential participants were being considered for enrollment in several protocols one or more of which allowed surrogate consent.

The finding that many individuals who lack the capacity to consent have the capacity to assign a surrogate to consent on their behalf is consistent with a task-specific conception of capacity. The study findings provide, as far as is known, the first estimate of how commonly the two capacities come apart.

### Contextualizing the study findings

Over the past decade and a half, the ratification of the Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (CRPD 2006) has brought to the fore a debate about the most appropriate approach for respecting the rights of disabled individuals. While surrogate decision-making had been the standard approach, supported decision-making has now become rather widely endorsed as offering greater legal protection of rights for individuals with cognitive disability24.

Do the study findings here contribute to this debate and if so how? It would seem to depend upon how one interprets the approach of the ACAT. The study findings suggest that the ACAT approach has yielded a high percentage of determinations that individuals with initially uncertain capacity to consent are either able to consent or able to assign a surrogate to consent on their behalf. Arguably, this would seem to represent quite a successful approach to respect for persons. But should the results be counted as evidence in favor of the substituted judgment model or as evidence in favor of the supported decision-making model?

One might consider the ACAT approach to consent for individuals whose capacity is in doubt as consistent with the surrogate decision-making model since the ACAT turns to a surrogate decision-maker to provide consent after a determination that an individual lacks the capacity to consent. As such, the study findings might be interpreted as yielding evidence in favor of the surrogate decision-making approach.

Yet, alternatively, one might make the case that the ACAT approach to consent for individuals whose capacity is in doubt as consistent with the supported decision-making model. The ACAT takes the sort of functional approach that the supported decision-making model endorses25. The team does not presume that an individual has a fixed status with regard to capacity to consent. The team promotes the opportunity for persons with cognitive disability to exercise their capacity to make decisions for themselves in several ways: carefully evaluating the ability to consent when there is any doubt, exploring whether they are able to assign a surrogate that they would prefer if they cannot consent themselves, and assessing surrogates to make sure they are able to represent the wishes of research participants. This is quite in contrast to a strict substituted judgment model that simply takes disabled status of an individual as a given.

Subsequent to the date of the last assessment included in this study, the NIH CC modified its policy regarding surrogate decision-making in research. The most recent version of this policy states that NOK can consent even if individuals cannot assign a surrogate. This revised policy may be less consistent with the move towards supported decision-making given that it is unknown whether the potential participant would have chosen the NOK as a surrogate as someone who knows and respects the research participant’s values and preferences.

### Implications for others

This study reports an approach to capacity assessments that maximizes the possibility of respectfully enrolling individuals whose ability to consent is compromised. While these findings are derived from review of practices pursued at the intramural research program at the NIH, the results should be of interest to clinical investigators at a wide range of research institutions as they pursue efforts to guarantee human subjects protection during the consent process.

How feasible might it be to utilize the approach reported here at various research institutions? The growing number of research institutions that have research ethics consultation services, might make it quite practicable to staff a process like the one described here. Alternatively, where that is not possible, the process used here might be adapted for use by others at smaller facilities.

It is also important to consider the additional safeguards necessary to protect potential participants who may be unable to consent for themselves. Although regulations meant to safeguard certain vulnerable populations may be silent with regard to assessment of the capacity to consent, the inclusion of such participants in research is of vital importance to science and necessary for the prevention, treatment and cure of debilitating conditions. The twenty years of experience and the recommendations shared by the consultation team at the NIH CC, serve as an example of how to address human subjects’ protections in an ethical manner. Research institutions, both large and small, can benefit from having an experienced team and/or consultants with specialized training in bioethics, mental health federal regulations and public health policies related to human subject protections.

The results of this study support participant-centered approaches and share both programmatic and concrete examples regarding how researchers can conduct responsible research. For example, a few protocols had differing levels of risk for potential participants with capacity and without capacity to consent to research - some procedures of higher risk were eliminated for incapacitated participants. This may provide a potential safeguard for potential participants to still be able to participate in research by adjusting the study procedures based on the capabilities of the prospective study population.

### Conclusion

The study results show that a substantial number of potential research participants whose ability consent is uncertain at the point of possible enrollment can be included in research with the involvement of an ability-to-consent assessment team. Results reveal that a very high fraction of individuals who were evaluated using this approach were either found to be able to consent on their own or to be able to assign a surrogate who could consent on their behalf. This study also highlights that well-established capacity assessment teams also facilitate the determination of the best alternative surrogate decision-maker who can consent to enrollment thus maximizing the self-determination and autonomy of the potential participant26.

# Exploring the Motivations of Research Participants Who Chose Not to Learn Medically Actionable Secondary Genetic Findings about Themselves

**Authors:** Will Schupmann; Skye A Miner; Haley K Sullivan; Jamie R Glover; Janet E Hall; Shepherd H Schurman; Benjamin E Berkman

**Affiliations:** 1NIH Department of Bioethics | 2NIH Department of Bioethics | 3Harvard University | 4Social and Scientific Systems | 5NIEHS Clinical Research Branch, NIEHS, NIH | 6NIEHS Clinical Research Branch, NIEHS, NIH | 7NIH Department of Bioethics, NHGRI

## Abstract

Proposals to return medically actionable secondary genetic findings (SFs) in the clinical and research settings have generated controversy regarding whether to solicit individuals’ preferences about their “right not to know” genetic information. This study contributes to the debate by surveying research participants who have actively decided whether to accept or refuse SFs.

Participants were drawn from a large NIH environmental health study. Participants who had accepted SFs (n=148) or refused SFs (n=83) were given more detailed information about the types of SFs researchers could return and were given an opportunity to revise their original decision.

41/83 initial refusers (49.4%) opted to receive SFs following the informational intervention. Nearly 75% of these “reversible refusers” thought they had originally accepted SFs. The 50.6% of initial refusers who continued to refuse (“persistent refusers”) demonstrated high levels of understanding of which SFs would be returned post-intervention. The most prominent reason for refusing was concern about becoming worried or sad (43.8%).

This study demonstrates the need for a more robust informed consent process when soliciting research participants’ preferences about receiving SFs. We also suggest that our data support implementing a default practice of returning SFs without actively soliciting preferences.

Keywords: secondary findings, right not to know, research ethics, informed consent

## Introduction

With the increasing adoption of whole genome and exome sequencing, researchers and clinicians have had to grapple with how to address the potential for uncovering findings unrelated to the primary sequencing objective (“secondary findings,” or “SFs” which have been distinguished from the broader category of “incidental findings” as information that is still unrelated to the research or clinical aim but are actively sought).1 In 2013, the American College of Medical Genetics and Genomics (“ACMG”) promulgated a list of genes in which disease causing variants should be returned to clinical genomic sequencing recipients without first soliciting their preferences about receiving this information.2,3 This proposal generated much debate around the so-called “right not to know” (“RNTK”) genetic information about oneself.4,5,6,7,8

Reflecting the dominant view, RNTK proponents argued that returning information to patients without soliciting their preferences is a violation of their autonomy.4-7,9,10,11 Even when this information is potentially life-saving, some argued, respecting autonomy ought to trump concerns of beneficence.4,5 In contrast, the ACMG argued that “clinicians have a fiduciary duty to warn patients about high-risk variants” and that it would not be “appropriate to give patients a choice not to learn about” these findings.3 This position has been extended to argue that the potential benefits of learning medically actionable genetic information far outweigh the harms, that support for the RNTK is inconsistent and malleable, and that the extremely small number of patients or research participants who choose to invoke the RNTK should not drive broad policies.3,12 Nonetheless, overwhelming criticism prompted the ACMG to revise their recommendations to allow patients “to opt out of the analysis of medically actionable genes” before their samples are sent for testing.13

Although distinct in some ways, a related debate is occurring among researchers who employ genomic sequencing regarding whether to solicit the informational preferences of study participants. In fact, resolving this controvery is perhaps more urgent in the research setting, where genomic sequencing has become exceedingly common. While different terms, such as “medically important genomic results,” have been proposed to distinguish actionable genetic findings that may surface in the research context from those in the clinical context, this study, which concerns the former, uses the term secondary findings.1

There are two areas where empirical research can inform this debate within the research context. First, proponents of soliciting research participants’ preferences assume that these preferences are strong and stable, and that they can reliably be captured during the consent process. However, studies on the quality of informed consent cast doubt on this assumption; there is significant variation in how people understand consent documents, and the way information is framed can have a significant impact on their understanding and answers.14,15 Therefore, it is critical to determine how strongly and consistently participants endorse the RNTK and how accurately preferences are captured during the consent process. Second, it is unclear why some participants refuse SFs. While some studies have explored refusers’ motivations,16,17,18,19 the data are largely qualitative and have sought respondents’ preferences and views in hypothetical scenarios, in part because the population of people not wanting to receive this information is so small.20 Thus, there has been a lack of generalizable data on the views and characteristics of people who have actively made the decision to refuse medically actionable genetic information.

Through an opportunity to survey a large group of research participants who made the decision not to receive SFs, this study aims to address these questions. Specifically, the study attempts to: (1) gauge the strength and stability of participants’ original decisions; (2) determine how informed participants were when they made their original decision; (3) ascertain whether more detailed information changes participants’ desires to receive SFs; (4) explore the reasoning employed by participants when making their choice about SFs; and (5) identify potential differences in reasons for refusal between racial and ethnic groups.

## Materials and Methods

Participants were drawn from the Environmental Polymorphisms Registry (EPR),21 an NIH study of 19,658 participants designed to examine how genetic and environmental factors influence human health, conducted by intramural investigators in the National Institute of Environmental Health Sciences (“NIEHS”; see [21] for more information on EPR’s recruitment strategies and the demographic characteristics of its participants). The consent form used language that has regularly been approved by IRBs, specifically stating that investigators “may find gene changes that are not related to this study” and that, with the participant’s consent, they would return findings when there is “a gene change that is important to you or your family’s health” (see “Original EPR Consent Language” in the supplementary materials). The EPR contacted participants in 2016 by email, mail and phone to get explicit permission for genomic sequencing and to solicit their preferences about whether or not to receive SFs. Non-responders were re-contacted in subsequent years using the same methods.

Of the participants who already had consented to genomic sequencing in the EPR at the time of our sub-study (which was open from November 18, 2019 to January 31, 2020), 8,678 elected to receive SFs, and 165 elected not to receive them. Our sub-study invited all 165 SF “refusers” as well as a random sample of 330 SF “acceptors”. The rate of SF refusal (the number of participants who refused SFs out of the total 8,843 participants who agreed to be sequenced and expressed a preference about knowing or not know) was significantly higher among Black participants (3.2%) compared to white participants (1.6%; odds ratio 2.07, 95% confidence interval 1.44 to 2.94, p=0.00006). To explore factors that may account for this higher rate of refusal (e.g., historical research abuses and subsequent broad distrust of the medical/research establishment) Black participants were oversampled in the acceptors cohort. Other than oversampling by race, acceptors were chosen at random from the EPR acceptors cohort. Participants were contacted about the online survey by text and email, with periodic reminders for initial non-responders.

Arguments in the literature for and against receiving genetic information about oneself were used to develop preliminary survey questions. The survey was piloted using 12 cognitive interviews with EPR participants, conducted by the social science research firm that assists the EPR with their umbrella study. The survey was structured into three parts. In the first part, participants were asked questions to gauge the strength of their original decision and their recall of details about the kinds of SFs that might be returned as described in the original consent form. In the second part (intervention), participants were provided more detailed information about the types of SFs researchers may return to participants, namely that SFs would only be returned if they were associated with serious disease, treatable, and had a strong evidence base (see “Intervention Text” in the supplementary materials). Participants were then given an opportunity to make a revised, binding decision about whether to receive SFs. In the third part, participants were asked questions about their new decision.

Data were analyzed using R software (version 3.6.2). Descriptive statistics were generated for the sample’s demographic characteristics (e.g., race, age, and gender) as well as participants’ responses to many of the survey’s questions, including those testing the strength and stability of their original decisions, their understanding of SFs, and their reasons for making their decisions. Bivariate analyses, including Pearson’s chi-squared test, McNemar’s test, Fisher’s exact test, and t test statistics, were subsequently used to explore differences in responses between acceptors and refusers, differences in responses before and after the survey’s intervention, and differences in responses between racial groups.

## Results

There were 231 responses out of a total 495 participants contacted, for a response rate of 46.7 percent. The response rate among refusers was slightly higher (83/165, 50.3 percent) than that of acceptors (148/330, 44.4 percent).

### Characteristics of Respondents’ Original Decision

Respondents characterized the strength and stability of their original decision (Table 1). When asked how well they remembered making their decision, 43.3 percent of respondents reported not remembering being asked the question at all or vaguely remembering being asked the question. Refusers may have been more likely not to have remembered making the decision (X2 [2, N = 231] = 5.467, p = 0.065). When asked what they thought their original decision had been, 45.8 percent of refusers thought they had accepted, while 6.8 percent of acceptors thought they had refused—meaning, when comparing one’s actual decision with one’s later reported recollection of that decision, concordance for refusers was significantly lower than concordance for acceptors (Fisher’s exact, p < 0.001). Most participants (80.1 percent) thought they had enough information to make their original decision, and a similar number (80.5 percent) had not thought about changing their decision since making it.

### Differences in Reasons for Refusal Between Racial and Ethnic Groups

Black respondents were significantly more likely to originally refuse to receive SFs than non-Black participants (including whites and Asian Americans)—47.4 percent refused, versus 31.7 percent of whites and Asian Americans (X2 [1, N = 224] = 3.868, p = 0.049) (see Table A: Demographics and Original Decision in supplemental materials). Refusers’ reasons were analyzed by race and found that Black respondents were more likely than non-Black respondents to refuse SFs in part because they did not trust the NIH with their genetic information; 11.1 percent of Black respondents endorsed this reason versus zero percent of whites and Asian Americans (p = 0.036) (Table 2).

### Respondents’ Decision Post-Intervention

Following the provision of more detailed information about SFs, there was a significant increase in the number of respondents accepting (McNemar’s test, X2 [1, 231] = 24.596, p < 0.001) (see Table 3). A total of 41 respondents switched from refusing to accepting, while six people switched from accepting to refusing—a net decrease in refusing of 42.2 percent. Of all respondents, 76.6 percent reported they were “completely” or “pretty sure” about their decision, and 93.9 percent reported they “had enough information” to make their decision—a 13.8 percent increase from before more information was provided.

### Characteristics of Respondents Who Refused Post-Intervention

There was no significant difference between the persistent and reversible refusers regarding whether they thought they had enough information (pre-intervention), but reversible refusers may have been more likely to have thought about changing their decision since (Fisher’s exact, p = 0.071). The level of understanding about SFs among persistent refusers was high; in fact, this group may have had a slightly better understanding in some respects than respondents who accepted post-intervention (Figure 1C). ## Discussion

This study contributes a number of important findings to the debate within the research setting on the right not to know genetic information about oneself. In turn, these findings point to several implications for policies governing the return of SFs to research participants.

We found that the group of participants in our sample who originally refused to receive SFs was equally divided between “reversible refusers” and “persistent refusers.” Reversible refusers switched their decision to accepting SFs following the intervention, while persistent refusers continued to refuse. Reversible refusers were significantly less likely to have remembered their original decision accurately and more likely to have thought about changing their original decision than persistent refusers. Despite the observation that refusers, on the whole, were less likely to have remembered their original decision than acceptors, persistent refusers not only had a more stable preference than reversible refusers, but they also had a high level of understanding of what SFs would include. In fact, persistent refusers may have had a higher level of understanding of SFs than acceptors, post-intervention.

These findings add nuance to the ethical and policy debates surrounding the RNTK genetic information about oneself. Scholars who have endorsed a more absolute conception of the RNTK argue that some research participants have a genuine preference not to know certain information about themselves, and that this preference ought to be respected. They advocate that these preferences be actively solicited as part of the consent process for genomic sequencing, instead of having a default practice of returning SFs.4 The critical assumption made here is that a participant’s indicated preference on a consent form reflects their true considered view.

On the one hand, our finding that many participants of genetic testing may initially refuse SFs but do not have strong or stable preferences calls this assumption into question. Rather, it suggests that consent form check boxes may not be the most appropriate method to solicit people’s preferences, and that decisions made in that context should not be seen as definitive expressions of preference. This point is emphasized by our finding that almost half of participants who initially refused SFs subsequently accepted them. By soliciting preferences through check boxes after an accurate but limited presentation of information, it is likely that some participants will make a choice that results in forgoing potentially life-saving information that, upon further reflection, they would have wanted to receive. On the other hand, this study found that some participants have strong convictions about not wanting to know certain genetic information about themselves, and moreover, that these “persistent refusers” continue to refuse despite a high level of understanding of SFs. By not soliciting preferences, these persistent refusers would potentially receive information that they genuinely do not want.

In order to minimize the number of people unintentionally refusing SFs while also respecting those who truly do not want to receive SFs, one path forward would be to implement a more robust informed consent process. By providing more detailed information about the types of genetic information that would and would not be returned, the indicated preferences of research participants would likely become more accurate. Another strategy would be to ask for people’s preferences at multiple timepoints. As will be discussed below, it is possible that our survey’s intervention—the provision of more detailed information—was not responsible for the increased uptake of SFs, but rather asking participants a second time was. Given how difficult it is to maintain contact with research participants, however, this strategy would pose a potentially significant logistical burden on research teams.

More controversially, our findings could also lend support for implementing a default practice of attempting to return medically actionable genetic findings to research participants, without actively soliciting preferences. While we found that approximately half of our sample of refusers continued to refuse even after more information was provided and that their preferences were stable and well-informed, it is important to put this finding into perspective. In the overall sample of EPR participants ~98% of the cohort initially agreed to receive SFs; this group of “persistent refusers” represents a very small proportion of the study population (less than 1%) which is consistent with what studies soliciting the hypothetical preferences of patients, participants, and the public have found about low SF refusal rates.15-17,22,23,24,25,26,27 While many bioethicists approach the RNTK debate primarily through an autonomy lens, our data suggest that an equally legitimate normative frame is to consider whether RNTK policies should be constructed to accommodate this very small group at the expense of a different small group of people who refuse SFs unintentionally or through misunderstanding and subsequently forgo potentially life-saving information. In light of our findings we argue that it is ethically acceptable to consider an approach where the explicitly articulated default is to attempt to return a defined set of high-value SFs, with an implicit mechanism for persistent refusers to self-identify as wanting to opt out of receiving SFs.3 The potentially significant harms of participants misreporting their preferences on a consent form and forgoing valuable health information outweighs the harms of not respecting the preferences of a handful of persistent refusers who do not opt-out. That many of the reasons for refusing SFs endorsed by persistent refusers are based on unfounded concerns—not including a historical mistrust of healthcare institutions and medical research (discussed below)—also supports this view.

While this study demonstrated an increase in accepting SFs following the provision of more detailed information about SFs, the relationship between being well-informed and one’s information preferences remains unclear. On the one hand, it appears that improving people’s understanding leads to a higher rate of accepting SFs, as “reversible refusers” demonstrated improved understanding following the provision of additional information and switched their decision from refusing to accepting. This correlation between being well-informed and wanting genetic information is consistent with other studies.28,29 On the other hand, it appears that many people still refuse despite a high level of understanding (the “persistent refusers” as described above), and acceptors don’t necessarily have high levels of understanding. When we compared the understanding of acceptors (pre- and post-intervention) with that of refusers (pre- and post-intervention), acceptors had poorer understanding, in some respects, than refusers at both timepoints. On the whole, acceptors thought incorrectly that findings would include more information than those who refused.

These contradictory findings suggest that being more informed is not the only factor that contributes to accepting SFs. That is, reversible refusers may be switching not only because they have become better informed, but also because they had more time to think about their decision and are being asked a second time.30 Further research is needed to understand how repeated solicitations of preferences about SFs influence decision-making, and whether the act of asking multiple times creates undue pressure on a person to accept SFs or enhances their autonomy by giving them a chance to reconsider. Additionally, acceptors may not be accepting because they are better informed about what SFs will include, but perhaps because this group is generally more information-seeking.27 More research is needed to understand the causal relationship between being better informed and wanting more health information about oneself, as well as the additional factors that make some people accept and some people refuse.

In revealing some of the justifications for why people accept or refuse SFs, this study also points to potential educational strategies researchers may use to further improve the consent process. Specifically, several of the reasons for refusing can potentially be addressed through provision of additional detail and context. The most common reason chosen for refusing was that the information might make the recipient worried or sad. The concern that learning genetic information will lead to psychological harms has been prominent in the bioethics literature,7 but more recent data suggest that people who have received troubling genetic information do not end up being as anxious as they thought they would be.31,32,33 Likewise, about 10 percent of refusers did so because they were worried their health insurance would use the information against them. Yet the Genetic Information Nondiscrimination Act (GINA) prohibits health insurers from doing precisely this, and there is little evidence to suggest that health insurers and employers have ever done this.34,35 About 10 percent of refusers also endorsed the reason that they did not think the information was relevant to their health. For this subset of people, this suggests a continued lack of understanding that the SFs would be medically actionable and evidence-based. Given that refusers may be basing their decision to forgo valuable health-promoting information on these potentially mitigatable concerns, it is worth considering strategies that researchers can use during the decision-making process to convey how resilient people are following information disclosure, the protections afforded by GINA, and the actionability of the information being returned.

Furthermore, a sizeable proportion of refusers made their decisions in part because they would not have done anything with the information (about 21 percent), and that they were not curious about the information (about 27 percent). More research needs to be done to understand why these reasons may have driven people not to receive important health information, and how researchers might address them. A notable finding was that very few refusers made their decision because they did not have access to healthcare, or because they were worried friends or family would treat them differently (i.e., stigma). This finding suggests that the significant attention given to stigma in the bioethics literature as a reason for not wanting to know genetic information may need to be reexamined.7,36 Additionally, it is important to note that six people switched from agreeing to refusing SFs as a result of this study. More research is also needed to understand why some people revoked their consent to receive SFs.

We analyzed reasons for refusing by race in an attempt to understand why a greater proportion of Black participants refused SFs and found that Black respondents were significantly more likely than whites and Asian Americans to endorse the idea that they did not trust NIH with their genetic information, both before and after the intervention. In fact, it was only Black respondents who chose this reason at both timepoints. Importantly, the absolute number of respondents who chose this reason is very small and thus unlikely to fully explain the racial difference in refusal. Nonetheless, decreased trust in healthcare institutions driving less healthcare utilization among Black people is consistent with what other studies have found.37,38,39,40 Higher distrust in the government’s regulation of research, and in researchers themselves, is driven by continued racial discrimination in the United States and historical medical injustices.39 This finding reminds us that it is important to be sensitive to the fact that there might be important and legitimate reasons for refusing that differ among racial groups.

### Limitations

There was a gap of more than a year between respondents making their original decision on whether to receive SFs and the administration of our survey. This may have resulted in our survey demonstrating a lower initial understanding of SFs than when respondents originally made their decision. This time gap also made it difficult to measure whether changes in understanding were due to the passage of time, or the provision of more detailed information about SFs. In addition, given the small numbers of participants in the specific racial and ethnic categories, one should be cautious about the statistical inferences about particular groups that can be drawn from the data. When analyzing by race, we compared Black respondants to whites and Asian Americans together. Yet there is little literature on the genetic information preferences or utilization of Asian Americans and thus there is some uncertainty about how to group them. Finally, though Black participants were significantly more likely to refuse SFs, that result was not strong (p = 0.049) and deserves further study.

### Conclusion

This study provides valuable data to inform how research institutions design policies related to returning SFs to research participants. Most significantly, our data raise questions about whether a strong conception of the “right not to know” is the right lens when creating policies to govern the return of SFs. We argue that our data support a default practice of attempting to return SFs without soliciting the preferences of research participants, while also providing a clearly-defined (though implicit) opt-out mechanism for people that independently raise concerns about the RNTK. An alternative policy could involve re-contacting refusers to provide them more time to make their decision and a chance to reconsider. The ability to re-query participants, however, would be logistically challenging and resource-intensive for many research teams. Our study shows that, at the very least, more detailed information about SFs should be provided to participants during the informed consent process. While further study is warranted, we believe that either of these policy choices would help decrease the number of research participants who inadvertently refuse important health information because of misunderstanding or indecision.

## Abstract

This economic evaluation examines the costs and benefits of cascade testing of siblings of newborns with cancer susceptibility gene variants.

## Introduction

Newborn population-based genetic screening may reduce pediatric cancer deaths and could be cost-effective.1 Testing siblings of newborns with variants (ie, cascade testing) could further improve population health.2 Economic studies of cascade testing have focused on adults, although evidence suggests that cost-effectiveness improves for some cancer syndromes when surveillance is initiated in younger individuals.3 Our objective was to estimate the benefits and costs of cascade testing of siblings of newborns with cancer susceptibility gene variants.

## Methods

This economic evaluation study followed the Consolidated Health Economic Evaluation Reporting Standards (CHEERS) reporting guideline. This study was deemed exempt from review, and informed consent was not required because the institutional review board at Harvard Pilgrim Health Care determined the project did not meet the definition of human participant research.

Using the Precision Medicine Policy and Treatment (PreEMPT) model1 created in 2020, we estimated outcomes in siblings of newborns who were born with pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants in 1 of 11 pediatric cancer genes (ie, RET, RB1, TP53, DICER1, SUFU, PTCH1, SMARCB1, WT1, APC, ALK, or PHOX2B). Genes were selected based on associations with increased risk of very early onset malignant neoplasm and available surveillance guidelines. Children with variants were assumed to have 1 newborn sibling, based on US Census Bureau data. In the base case, we assumed de novo variants were rare, and siblings had 50% likelihoods of having the same germline variants as probands. Because of the variation and uncertainty in de novo variant rates by gene,4 we then varied assumptions about having the same germline variants to 5% (ie, very high de novo rate) and 25% (ie, moderate rate) in scenario analyses. Model outcomes included lifetime cancer deaths averted and cost-effectiveness relative to no cascade testing, calculated from a societal perspective with 3% discounting for costs and life-years (LYs). Cascade testing costs included Sanger sequencing (ie, $200) and clinical visits (ie, $188) before initiating surveillance. Surveillance costs were based on 2018 Medicare reimbursement rates. Sensitivity analyses varied costs of sequencing, clinical visits, and surveillance by 25%. To capture uncertainty, we conducted 1000 simulations where we sampled model parameters from their underlying distributions. We report means and 95% uncertainty intervals (UIs), defined as the 2.5 and 97.5 percentiles of estimates from 1000 simulations. Analyses were conducted in 2021 using R version 4.1.0 (R Project for Statistical Computing). Statistical tests were not conducted, given estimates were derived from simulation modeling rather that population sampling.

## Discussion

In this study, we estimated that sibling cascade testing would identify approximately 800 siblings with variants, avert half of projected cancer deaths before age 20 years among these individuals, and would have high value.5 Results align with adult studies that find relatives’ genetic testing cost-effective compared with standard screening.2

Limitations to our work included consideration of only 11 genes, exclusion of costs and benefits of parental cascade testing, entry of siblings into the model at birth, and omission of impact on adult-onset cancer outcomes. Benefits assumed full adherence to surveillance and previously used assumptions regarding early detection resulting in improved outcomes.1 We did not consider how siblings of variant carriers who developed cancer may already undergo surveillance or genetic testing. Notably, the most cancer deaths averted (ie, 80%-89%) accrued among siblings of healthy newborns. Findings demonstrate how sibling cascade testing would enhance newborn screening efforts and how targeted screening approaches may be more efficient than universal screening to achieve population-level benefits.6
